paras: The Prineville vigilante killings were the shooting of A. C. Swartz and the hanging of Sid Huston and Charles Luster by masked men at Prineville, Crook County, Oregon, on a night shortly before Christmas 1882. All three were accused of belonging to an organized band of horse thieves, and the killings were attributed to a vigilance committee of stockmen. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a lynching of desperate cowboys, while an Oregon paper condemned it as murder.

According to correspondence from Prineville printed through The Dalles, stock raisers around Prineville and Beaver Creek had complained for years of horse thefts, estimated at nearly 500 head over two years, and about thirty head had recently been driven off toward the John Day country. The correspondent described the thieves as an organized band scattered across eastern Oregon whose members were almost impossible to catch or convict. The stockmen organized, and the capture of some of the band's 'weakest' members and 'a judicious use of the rope' produced a confession naming the rest, with Swartz and John Thorp identified as the local leaders.

Swartz, learning that the scheme had leaked out, was said to have come into town and threatened to shoot anyone who interfered with his party. That evening, while he sat at a card table in Burmeister's saloon, someone standing outside shot him through the neck through the window, and he later died of the wound. The same night a band of masked men broke into the house of W. C. Barnes near Prineville and seized Huston, formerly of Linn County, and Luster, recently from California.

The two men were taken about a mile, or by the State Rights Democrat's account two miles toward Ochoco, and found hanged to the limb of a juniper tree. Huston had been shot once in the head and Luster twice, and the Albany paper judged that 'the shooting was probably done after they were hung.'

The Dalles dispatch said the identity of the 'executioners' was a matter of conjecture and that the act appeared to have the 'hearty approval of the entire community.' John Thorp, Price Thorp and James Townsend, named as the rest of the band, had escaped with vigilantes on their trail. No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The story reached national papers on December 28 in two forms: a brief Portland report that three 'cowboys of a desperate character' had been lynched 'on general principles,' and the longer Dalles particulars. Headline writers framed it as rough justice, under titles such as 'Hung for the Public Good,' 'A Neck-tie Party' and 'A PARTY OF HORSE THIEVES TREAT- ED TO THE ROPE IN OREGON.' Transmission garbled the details: papers in Washington, New York and New Haven moved the event to 'Pineville' in Wyoming Territory, one item placed it at Portland, and condensed texts invented a victim named 'J. Weston.'

Oregon papers wrote from closer sources and in a different tone. The State Rights Democrat of Albany called it a 'terrible tragedy' in which 'a Linnite, a Marionite and a Californian lost their lives,' and corrected that the Swartz killed was not the former Albany resident of that name. The Douglas Independent of Roseburg described a 'reign of terror' in the new county and declared that 'mob law is never justifiable in any civilized community,' urging that the killers be punished for murder. No paper in the coverage gave the race of any of the dead men.

The date varies by source: the first Portland report said Monday night, most reprints of the Dalles dispatch said 'last Friday night,' and the State Rights Democrat said 'last Saturday.' The Seattle Post-Intelligencer's fuller text dated the Prineville letter December 24 and placed the killings the previous night, which agrees with the Saturday date. Accounts also differ on the count, from 'three men' lynched to a 'lynching of two cowboys,' a difference that turns on whether Swartz's shooting is counted with the hangings.

reader.title: Prineville vigilante killings (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A band of masked men took Sid Huston and Charles Luster from a house near Prineville and hanged and shot them as alleged horse thieves, the same night A. C. Swartz was shot through a saloon window (A2, A25, A28).

Huston and Luster were seized by 'a band of masked men' acting for a stockmen's vigilance committee and hanged without any legal process on the accusation of horse stealing (A2, A25, A37); no number of lynchers is printed, but the papers describe a band and a committee.

The Dalles dispatch from Prineville correspondence (A2, A28) and the State Rights Democrat's account from a Prineville letter and the Prineville News (A25) agree on the shooting of Swartz and the hanging of Huston and Luster.

accounts.label: First Portland wire
accounts.gist: Three 'cowboys of a desperate character' were lynched at Prineville on Monday night 'on general principles'; nothing else was known.

accounts.label: Prineville correspondence via The Dalles
accounts.gist: Stockmen who had tracked an organized horse-thief band forced confessions with a rope; Swartz was shot in a saloon and masked men hanged and shot Huston and Luster, with community approval and vigilantes hunting the rest.

accounts.label: Prineville letter and Prineville News
accounts.gist: On 'last Saturday' Swartz was shot during a card game and died, and Huston and Luster were found hanged to a juniper two miles toward Ochoco; the News gave horse stealing as the 'generally accepted reason' and the paper called it the work of the 'Vigilante Committee.'

accounts.label: Douglas Independent editorial
accounts.gist: A stockmen's vigilance committee killed the three; mob law is never justifiable and the killers should be punished for murder.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Portland brief ('LYNCHED ON GENERAL PRINCIPLES', 'Three Desperate Cow-Boys Lynched') or the Dalles particulars without comment.
Headlines such as 'Hung for the Public Good', 'A Neck-tie Party' and 'A PARTY OF HORSE THIEVES TREAT- ED TO THE ROPE' presented the hangings as deserved.
The Seattle text of the Prineville letter said the town was 'shocked and horrified' yet, 'horrible as it seems,' the community approved.
The Douglas Independent called it a 'bloody deed' and demanded punishment for murder.

versions.value: Night of Dec. 23 (letter dated Dec. 24, 'Last night'; 'last Saturday')

conflicts.note: The Monday date comes from a first Portland report that knew only that a lynching had happened. The Seattle text appears to preserve the original letter (dated Dec. 24, 'Last night'), which agrees with the State Rights Democrat's 'last Saturday', so Dec. 23 has the best support; the Sacramento text gives the letter date as Dec. 27 and 'Last Friday night'.

versions.value: Two hanged and one shot (Swartz), all three dead

conflicts.note: The Oregon papers count Swartz, killed by a shot through a window, with the two men hanged.
The dispatch itself is datelined The Dalles and speaks of eastern Oregon; the Wyoming placement is an eastern editing error.

versions.value: Huston shot once through the head and Luster twice
'J. Weston was also shot thrice through the head'

conflicts.note: 'J. Weston' appears only in condensed wire texts at the point where the fuller texts describe Huston's and Luster's wounds; it is probably a telegraphic garble, not a fourth victim.
The fuller texts give Thorp and also name a Price Thorp.
